title: SYSK's 12 Days of Christmas… Toys: What Makes a Must-Have Christmas Toy?
summary: Holiday playlist episode of Stuff You Should Know ("SYSK's 12 Days of Christmas... Toys") asking what makes a must-have Christmas toy. The hosts argue Cabbage Patch Kids (1983) or earlier Star Wars empty-box Early Bird certificates started the trend, then survey past must-have toys (Nintendo consoles, Tickle Me Elmo, Hatchimals, Fingerlings). They credit scarcity marketing, holiday advertising, and buzz as drivers, discuss toy-flipping and bots that buy out restocks, how retailer toy lists (Amazon, Walmart, Target) are compiled and sometimes paid for, and close with a rundown of this year's hot toys such as Bloom Dolls, Hatchimals, Barbie Dream Plane, L.O.L. Surprise, Lego movie kit, and Fisher-Price Little People animals. Ends with listener mail from a teacher.

segments.title: Holiday playlist intro
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the episode as part of a December 12 Days of Christmas Toys playlist of toy-centric episodes. Hosts open with banter about early holiday retail.
topics: Stuff You Should Know Christmas playlist

segments.title: Opening banter on Cabbage Patch Kids
segments.summary: Hosts reminisce about 1983 Christmas toys; Josh mentions his sister's Little People doll made by Xavier Roberts, and they discuss whether Cabbage Patch Kids were the first must-have toy.

segments.title: Debate: first must-have Christmas toy
segments.summary: Chuck argues Cabbage Patch Kids created the must-have Christmas toy concept, citing earlier hits like Mister Potato Head and Robert the Robot. Josh counters that Star Wars' empty early bird box, sold in large numbers after Kenner underestimated demand, was earlier.

segments.title: Atari Pac-Man and violent toy crowds
segments.summary: Josh cites Atari Pac-Man cartridges as his childhood must-have. Chuck points to violent toy-buying crowds as a marker of must-have status, and the hosts conclude Cabbage Patch Kids fit the pattern with supply shortages and media buzz.

segments.title: Hallmarks of must-have toys: Nintendo, Tickle Me Elmo, Hatchimals
segments.summary: Hosts list Nintendo hits in 1988, 1989 and 1993, plus N64 and GoldenEye. Chuck describes Tickle Me Elmo in 1996 causing a Walmart employee to be trampled. Hosts briefly confuse Hatchimals with another egg toy, then Chuck clarifies how they work.

segments.title: Question: how does a toy become must-have
segments.summary: Chuck poses the central question of how a toy becomes a must-have Christmas toy, noting media coverage but little research on it.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the content resumes.

segments.title: Wishbooks, catalogs and modern toy lists
segments.summary: Hosts recall Sears Wishbook and Montgomery Ward catalogs and the Wishbook web site, which has scanned catalogs up to 1996. They note that modern toy lists from retailers and third-party sites have replaced department store catalogs.

segments.title: Paid placement on toy lists
segments.summary: Discussion of retailer toy lists, including reports that Amazon charges for nomination to its hot-toy list and that Walmart charges per toy for its Buyers Picks list. Target's list appears not to charge. The hosts note that third-party lists should disclose their methods and that sponsored results can be hard to tell apart.

segments.title: Holiday marketing and kids' advertising
segments.summary: Josh says marketers exploit happy holiday moods. He cites a University of Hertfordshire study counting about 100 ads in a three-hour Saturday morning kids slot. Chuck calls holiday-themed ads basic marketing.

segments.title: Scarcity marketing
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck explain scarcity marketing: limited supply triggers fear of missing out and frenzy. Chuck describes fear of social embarrassment and the haves and have-nots dynamic during the holidays.

segments.title: Limited releases, Disney Vault and Hatchimals shortage claims
segments.summary: Hosts discuss limited-release tactics such as the Disney Vault and Pappy Van Winkle whiskey. They describe Spin Master's Hatchimals shortages, which were accused of being deliberate scarcity marketing, and Fingerlings, where the maker added factories and air freight to meet demand.

segments.title: Scarcity examples in food and restaurants
segments.summary: Josh cites a restaurant burger released in limited numbers and a supermarket sign limiting soup purchases to twelve per person as examples of scarcity tactics.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the toy-flipper discussion.

segments.title: Toy flippers and bots
segments.summary: Hosts debate toy flippers who buy hot toys to resell at a markup. Chuck accepts professional flipping less than occasional resale; Josh objects to flipping and to bots that buy out stock and resell. They describe bots refreshing product pages and buying out inventory. Josh also mentions a show-tickets aside about listener spots.

segments.title: Reselling tips and Michael Larson comparison
segments.summary: Chuck summarizes an Investopedia guide to reselling toys at Christmas, including asking parents, kids, mall Santas and store staff about upcoming restocks, and online groups. The hosts compare this to Michael Larson's Press Your Luck strategy.

segments.title: Competition from resellers
segments.summary: Chuck says resellers actively contribute to scarcity and drive the frenzy. Josh jokes about dating a toy flipper.

segments.title: This year's hot toys
segments.summary: Hosts cross-referenced lists from Target, Toys R Us, Amazon, the Today Show, Toy Insider, The Spruce, Walmart, New York Magazine and others. Bloom Dolls appeared on the most lists. Other picks include Hatchimals, the How to Train Your Dragon Toothless Hatchimals, Barbie Dream Plane, L.O.L. Surprise, unboxing YouTube trend, Ryan's World, Lego make-your-own movie kit, Fisher-Price Little People animals and Playmobil.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh wrap up, joking about buying toys and flipping Hatchimals.

segments.title: Listener mail from a teacher
segments.summary: A teacher named John Lubushkin says his students enjoy the hosts' recurring characters used in class, and he encourages the hosts to keep sharing strong opinions. The hosts also invite feedback by email and social media.
